title: The Inverse of a Square Matrix

blocks.title: What is an Inverse Matrix?
teacherCues: Write $2 \times 2$ matrices $A$ and $B$ where $AB = I$. Ask: How are $A$ and $B$ related?
Emphasize that not every square matrix has an inverse; if it does, it's called invertible or nonsingular.

discoveryHook.scenario: Just like $5^{-1} = \frac15$ undoes multiplication by 5, an inverse matrix undoes the effect of multiplying by the original matrix.

explanation: For a square matrix $A$, if there exists a matrix $A^{-1}$ such that $AA^{-1} = I$ and $A^{-1}A = I$, then $A^{-1}$ is the [[kw:inverse]] of $A$.
Only square matrices can have inverses; a nonsquare matrix cannot have an inverse.
A matrix that has an inverse is called [[kw:invertible]] (or nonsingular). If no inverse exists, it is singular.
To verify that $B$ is the inverse of $A$, check that $AB = I$ and $BA = I$.

formulaCard.title: Inverse Definition
notes: The identity matrix $I$ has 1s on the main diagonal and 0s elsewhere.
Verify both products — they must equal the identity matrix.

examples.title: A – Verify an Inverse
examples.prompt: Show that $B = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$ is the inverse of $A = \begin{bmatrix} -1 & 2 \\ 1 & -1 \end{bmatrix}$.
steps: So $AB = I$. Check $BA$ similarly and you'll also get $I$.

examples.title: B – Is the inverse unique?
examples.prompt: If a matrix has an inverse, is it unique? Explain why.
examples.peerPrompt: Suppose $B$ and $C$ are both inverses of $A$. Multiply $AB = I$ by $C$ on the left and see what happens.
steps: $AB = I$. Multiply both sides on the left by $C$: $C(AB) = CI$.
$(CA)B = C$ because matrix multiplication is associative.
But $CA = I$, so $IB = C$, hence $B = C$.

examples.title: C – Quick check
examples.prompt: If $AA^{-1} = I$, does it automatically guarantee $A^{-1}A = I$? (Yes or No)
steps: For square matrices, yes: if $AB = I$, then $BA = I$ also holds. So checking one product is sufficient.

confusionCorner.title: Not all matrices are invertible
confusionCorner.body: If a matrix has a row or column of zeros, or if its determinant is zero, it is singular (no inverse).

questions.prompt: The inverse of a matrix $A$ is denoted $A$ raised to the power ___.
The product of a matrix and its inverse is the ___ matrix.
If $AB = I$, then $B$ is the ___ of $A$.
hints: It undoes the effect of A.

blocks.title: Finding the Inverse (Gauss‑Jordan Method)
teacherCues: Write a 2×2 matrix A and adjoin the identity: [A | I]. Show row operations until left side becomes I.
Emphasize that we perform the same operations on the entire augmented matrix. If the left can't become I, A is singular.

discoveryHook.scenario: Finding an inverse by hand is like solving a puzzle: you build the identity matrix step by step using row operations, and whatever appears on the right side is the inverse.

explanation: To find $A^{-1}$, set up the augmented matrix $[A \mid I]$ and use [[kw:Gauss‑Jordan elimination]] to transform the left side into $I$.
The right side will then become $A^{-1}$: $[A \mid I] \rightarrow [I \mid A^{-1}]$.
If the left side cannot be reduced to $I$ (e.g., a row of zeros appears), then $A$ has no inverse (singular).

formulaCard.title: Gauss‑Jordan Inverse Method
formulaCard.formula: Form $[A \mid I]$. Row reduce to $[I \mid A^{-1}]$.
notes: Use elementary row operations (swap, multiply, add multiple).
If a row of zeros appears on the left before reaching I, A is singular.

examples.title: B – 3×3 Inverse (partially)
examples.prompt: Set up the augmented matrix for $A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & -1 \\ 6 & -2 & -3 \end{bmatrix}$ and perform the first row operation to create zeros below the first pivot.
examples.peerPrompt: Which row operations will eliminate the 1 and 6 in the first column? Apply them.

examples.title: C – Quick check
examples.prompt: If during Gauss‑Jordan elimination you get a row of zeros on the left side (before the vertical line), what does that indicate?
steps: It means the matrix is singular (not invertible).

confusionCorner.title: Left side must become I
confusionCorner.body: The goal is to turn the original matrix (left half) into the identity matrix. If you end up with a row of zeros, the inverse does not exist.

questions.prompt: To find $A^{-1}$ using Gauss‑Jordan elimination, you adjoin the ___ matrix to $A$ before row reducing.
hints: Has 1s on the diagonal and 0s elsewhere.

questions.prompt: In the 2×2 example, after the first row operation, the entry in row 2, column 1 became ___.
hints: The goal is to create zeros below the diagonal.

questions.prompt: If the left side cannot be reduced to $I$, then the matrix is ___.

blocks.title: 2×2 Inverse Formula
teacherCues: Write $A = \begin{bmatrix} a & b \\ c & d \end{bmatrix}$ and the formula $A^{-1} = \frac{1}{ad-bc} \begin{bmatrix} d & -b \\ -c & a \end{bmatrix}$.
Explain that $ad-bc$ is the determinant; if it is zero, the matrix has no inverse.

discoveryHook.scenario: For 2×2 matrices, there is a quick formula: swap the diagonal entries, change the signs of the off‑diagonals, and divide by the determinant. It's like a recipe that always works—unless the determinant is zero, in which case the inverse doesn't exist.

explanation: For a 2×2 matrix $A = \begin{bmatrix} a & b \\ c & d \end{bmatrix}$, the inverse is $A^{-1} = \frac{1}{ad-bc} \begin{bmatrix} d & -b \\ -c & a \end{bmatrix}$, provided $ad-bc \neq 0$.
The quantity $ad-bc$ is called the [[kw:determinant]]. If the determinant is zero, the matrix is singular (no inverse).
Steps: swap $a$ and $d$, change signs of $b$ and $c$, then multiply by $\frac{1}{ad-bc}$.

formulaCard.title: 2×2 Inverse Formula
notes: If $ad-bc = 0$, the matrix is not invertible.

examples.title: B – When is it not invertible?
examples.prompt: For what values of $k$ does the matrix $\begin{bmatrix} 2 & k \\ 4 & 8 \end{bmatrix}$ fail to have an inverse?
examples.peerPrompt: Compute the determinant and set it equal to zero. Solve for $k$.
steps: So if $k=4$, the matrix is singular.

examples.title: C – Quick inverse
examples.prompt: Find the inverse of $\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 \end{bmatrix}$ using the formula.

confusionCorner.title: Don't forget to multiply by the reciprocal
confusionCorner.body: After swapping and changing signs, you must multiply the entire matrix by $\frac{1}{ad-bc}$. Skipping this step gives a wrong answer.

questions.prompt: For the 2×2 inverse formula, the denominator $ad-bc$ is called the ___.
In the matrix $\begin{bmatrix} a & b \\ c & d \end{bmatrix}$, after applying the formula, the entry that replaces $a$ (top‑left) is ___.
If the determinant of a 2×2 matrix is 0, the matrix is ___.

blocks.title: Solving Systems Using Inverse Matrices
teacherCues: Write $AX = B$. Multiply both sides by $A^{-1}$ on the left: $X = A^{-1}B$.
Explain that this works only when $A$ is square and invertible, giving a unique solution.

discoveryHook.scenario: If you have a system of equations in matrix form $AX = B$, and you know the inverse of $A$, you can find the solution instantly by multiplying $A^{-1}B$ — just like solving $ax = b$ gives $x = a^{-1}b$.

explanation: A square linear system $AX = B$ has a unique solution if $A$ is invertible: $X = A^{-1}B$.
Steps: 1. Write the system as $AX = B$. 2. Find $A^{-1}$ (by Gauss‑Jordan or formula). 3. Multiply $A^{-1}$ by $B$ to get $X$.
If $A$ is singular, the system either has no solution or infinitely many.

formulaCard.title: Solving with Inverse
notes: Multiply the inverse on the left of $B$.
Check that $A$ is square and invertible.

examples.title: A – Solve 2×2 system
examples.prompt: Solve $\begin{cases} x + y = 5 \\ 2x + y = 7 \end{cases}$ using the inverse matrix.

examples.title: B – Why multiply on the left?
examples.prompt: Explain why we must multiply $B$ by $A^{-1}$ on the left, not the right.
examples.peerPrompt: Consider dimensions: $A$ is $n\times n$, $X$ and $B$ are $n\times 1$. $A^{-1}A = I$, so $A^{-1}(AX) = (A^{-1}A)X = X$. If we multiplied on the right, we'd get $AXA^{-1}$ which is not $X$.
steps: $AX = B$. Multiply both sides on left by $A^{-1}$: $A^{-1}(AX) = A^{-1}B$.
Thus $X = A^{-1}B$. Multiplication on the right would not simplify.

examples.title: C – Quick solve
examples.prompt: Use the inverse to solve $\begin{cases} 2x + 3y = 4 \\ x + 2y = 3 \end{cases}$.

confusionCorner.title: Order of multiplication
confusionCorner.body: Always multiply $A^{-1}$ on the left: $A^{-1}B$, not $BA^{-1}$. Matrix multiplication is not commutative.

questions.prompt: To solve $AX = B$ using the inverse, multiply both sides on the ___ by $A^{-1}$.
In the first example, what is the value of $x$? (Enter a number)
If $A$ is singular (no inverse), the system $AX = B$ does not have a ___ solution.
hints: It may have none or many.
The word means 'one and only one'.
questions.feedbackIfWrong: It does not have a unique solution.

blocks.title: Blueprint Aid – Application: Investment Distribution
teacherCues: Pose: An investment of $10,000 in three accounts at 6%, 7.5%, and 9.5% yields total interest $730. Also, the amount in the 9.5% account equals the amount in the 6% account minus the amount in the other. Solve using inverse.
Set up matrix equation $AX = B$ and find $A^{-1}$ to get solution.

discoveryHook.scenario: A financial planner needs to allocate $10,000 among three funds with different rates to earn $730 interest, with a condition on the high-risk fund. Representing the constraints as $AX = B$, finding $A^{-1}$ gives the exact dollar amounts instantly.

explanation: [[imp:Understand]]: Write the system in matrix form $AX = B$, where $A$ is the coefficient matrix, $X$ is the variables column, $B$ is the constants.
[[imp:Solve]]: Compute $A^{-1}$ using Gauss‑Jordan (or later technology). Then $X = A^{-1}B$.
[[imp:Conclude]]: The solution gives the amounts in each account.

formulaCard.title: Solving AX = B with Inverse
notes: The inverse can be reused for different $B$ with same $A$.

examples.title: A – Set up the system
examples.prompt: Write the matrix equation for the investment problem.

examples.title: B – Solve using A^{-1} given
examples.prompt: Suppose we are given $A^{-1} = \begin{bmatrix} 15 & -200 & 2 \\ -21.5 & 300 & -3.5 \\ 7.5 & -100 & 1.5 \end{bmatrix}$. Compute $X = A^{-1}B$.
examples.peerPrompt: Multiply the inverse matrix by the constant column. Work together.

confusionCorner.title: Inverse must be on the left

questions.prompt: In the matrix equation $AX = B$, the matrix $A$ contains the ___ of the variables.
In the investment problem, what was the amount invested at 9.5%? (Enter a number, no comma)
hints: The smallest of the three amounts.

questions.prompt: If the coefficient matrix is invertible, the system has a ___ solution.

challengeCorner.prompt: Solve the system $2x + 3y + z = -1$, $3x + 3y + z = 1$, $2x + 4y + z = -2$ using the inverse method (if you have the inverse, multiply). Should yield $x=2, y=-1, z=-2$.
hints: Set up $A$ and $B$, find $A^{-1}$ (or use given).
